item.title: Jensen Huang forfeits $108 million in unvested Nvidia equity
item.description: The relinquished awards represent roughly 0.08% of his net worth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, which puts his fortune at $138.4 billion.
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Jensen Huang will forfeit about $108 million in unvested equity compensation after being ousted from Nvidia Corp. — a fraction of his total wealth.The relinquished awards represent roughly 0.08% of his net worth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, which puts his fortune at $138.4 billion.The company’s equity compensation policy specifies that unvested RSUs, or restricted stock units, are forfeited once an executive terminates continuous service. He holds about 346,000 such units and would receive about 310,000 shares through the company’s equity incentive plan, assuming its performance meets certain targets.Unlike many other tech CEOs, Huang’s wealth is derived almost entirely from his holding of Nvidia’s common shares, rather than stock options or other forms of equity compensation. Huang controls about a 3.5% voting stake in the Santa Clara, California-based firm, which makes up nearly 97% of his wealth, according to Bloomberg’s wealth index.Since Nvidia only has one class of shares, Huang doesn’t hold any privileged voting rights.The 63-year-old co-founder, who stepped down following the revelation of two extramarital affairs, was paid about $7.5 million in cash compensation in each of the past two years — a negligible sum relative to his net worth. Still, his resignation came at an immediate cost. Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14% in New York before paring losses to close down 4.3% at $166.19, wiping more than $6 billion from Huang’s net worth.

item.title: Global bond yields surge to multi-year highs as inflation, borrowing concerns mount
item.description: Government bond yields globally rose to multi-decade highs recently due to sell-offs in sovereign debt. Investors demanded higher returns amid persistent inflation and uncertainty regarding interest rates. India's benchmark 10-year bond yield peaked at 7.50% before slightly declining to 7.24%. Recent easing geopolitical tensions and declining crude prices have supported bond market recovery. Nonetheless, the outlook remains uncertain due to inflationary pressures and concerns over fiscal sustainability.
item.dc:creator: Rozebud Gonsalves
item.content:encoded: Mumbai: A sell-off in sovereign debt pushed government bond yields across major economies to multiyear and, in some cases, multi-decade highs in the past month, as investors demanded higher returns to compensate for elevated government borrowing, sticky inflation and uncertainty over the interest-rate outlook.The US 10-year Treasury yield was at its highest since 2002, while Japanese government bond yields touched levels last seen in 1996. The repricing reverberated across global fixed-income markets.135785354India has not been immune, with the benchmark 10-year bond yield climbing to a four-year high of 7.50% in October before easing, to close around 7.24% on Thursday.Pressure on global bond markets has eased in recent weeks, with investors finding elevated yields attractive for fresh buying. Easing of the US-Iran war and the subsequent moderation in crude oil prices have also supported the recovery in government bonds by tempering inflation concerns.Read more: Meesho block deal: SoftBank-backed entity likely to sell 1% stake worth Rs 1,174 croreHowever, the outlook for global bond markets remains uncertain. Persistent inflationary pressures and expectations of tighter monetary policy across major economies are likely to keep yields elevated. Meanwhile, concerns over rising government borrowing requirements and fiscal sustainability are expected to sustain higher term premiums, limiting the scope for a meaningful decline in long-term yields, according to a Morgan Stanley report last week.Indian yields too are expected to be volatile. The 10-year G-Sec yield at around 7.55-7.60% offers an attractive entry point from a medium-term perspective. However, given the possibility of near-term swings in yields, accumulation should be staggered over the next three months rather than undertaken at a single point, according to Devang Shah, head of fixed income at Axis Mutual Fund.Read more: New SIP registrations fall 20%, stoppage ratio climbs to 116% in October after 5-month declineThe US 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.34% in October, its highest since 2002. The UK 10-year gilt yield rose to 5.378% on September 10, the highest since July 2007. It subsequently climbed to 5.52% on October 8. Germany's 10-year Bund yield touched 3.65% in early October, its highest since June 2009, while Japan's 10-year government bond yield hit 3.13% on October 1, a level last seen in 1996, according to Bloomberg.
